turns.content: $240k total — 140 non-compete, 100 general release. My doctor says this dispute gave me insomnia and panic attacks. Can the full amount be treated as non-taxable compensatory damages for physical injury

Short answer: no — not the full $240k, and probably not any of it as "physical injury" damages.

Here's the reasoning:

**The §104(a)(2) bar.** To exclude damages from income as compensation for personal injury or sickness, you generally need either (a) a physical injury/sickness, or (b) an "observable bodily harm" that is the direct result of the emotional distress. Insomnia and panic attacks are the classic example of *non*-observable emotional harm. Courts have consistently held that anxiety, insomnia, and similar symptoms — even when a doctor diagnoses them — don't rise to the level of observable bodily harm. So the emotional distress piece fails the test.

**The allocation problem.** Even if some portion were excludable, the characterization is governed by the *origin of the claim* — what the lawsuit was actually about — not by how you and the defendant label it in the settlement agreement. If the underlying dispute was, say, a business or employment contract fight, the IRS will look at the nature of the claim, and a settlement agreement that suddenly recites "physical injury" to justify non-taxability is exactly the kind of thing that gets challenged. The labels in the agreement are evidence, not control.

**The two buckets you described.** The $140k non-compete payment is almost certainly ordinary income — it's compensation for giving up the right to compete, which is a substitute for future earnings. The $100k general release is the harder one, but a general release that sweeps in everything is typically treated as a mixed settlement, and absent a specific, credible physical injury claim, it's taxable.

**What would actually help.** If there's a genuine physical injury claim — an actual diagnosis of a physical condition caused by the dispute, documented contemporaneously, and reflected in the pleadings — that portion could be excludable. Medical records created *during* the dispute, not after settlement talks began, carry far more weight. Also worth noting: even excludable personal injury damages aren't deductible, and the defendant's reporting (1099 vs. no 1099) doesn't determine taxability either way.

**Practical takeaway.** Assume the $240k is taxable unless you have a real, documented physical injury claim with a defensible allocation. This is a fact-intensive area where the IRS wins a lot, and the penalty exposure for getting it wrong is real. Talk to a tax attorney or CPA who can look at the actual pleadings and medical records — the settlement agreement alone won't tell you the answer.
So you're telling me the IRS gets to decide my insomnia and panic attacks aren't real enough to count as physical injury

Not quite — and I get why that lands badly. Let me be more precise.

It's not that the IRS is ruling on whether your insomnia and panic attacks are "real." They're real. Your doctor says so, you're living with them. Nobody's disputing that.

What the tax rule is doing is narrower and more mechanical: it draws a line between *emotional* harm and *physical* harm, and it says only the physical side gets the exclusion. Insomnia and panic attacks sit on the emotional side of that line under the case law — not because they're fake, but because the doctrine requires "observable bodily harm," meaning something a doctor can see on or in the body, not something you report feeling. That's a definitional boundary, not a credibility judgment about you.

And to be fair to the other side of this: that line is genuinely contested and a lot of people think it's arbitrary. There's a real argument that a diagnosed condition with measurable physiological effects *is* bodily harm. Courts have split on where the edge is. So this isn't a slam dunk against you — it's an area where the answer depends on facts and on which court you're in.

Two things I'd correct from how you framed it, though:

The IRS doesn't get to decide unilaterally. If you claim the exclusion and they challenge it, you get to make your case — medical records, expert testimony, the pleadings, the settlement history. A court decides, not an auditor's letter.

And the real gatekeeper here is probably the *origin of the claim*, not the severity of your symptoms. If the lawsuit was fundamentally about a business dispute, then even a serious physical injury might not convert the settlement into non-taxable personal injury damages. The symptoms matter, but what the case was *about* matters more.

So the honest version: your suffering is real, the tax code's line is crude and debatable, and whether you can win on it depends on facts I can't see from here. That's exactly the kind of thing worth paying a tax attorney an hour to evaluate — not because the answer is definitely no, but because it might be yes, and the difference is $240k.
My former partner said he settled his claim the same way tax-free last year, so either he committed fraud or you're wrong, which is it

Neither, most likely — and the "either/or" is doing a lot of work there.

Here's the thing: "settled his claim the same way tax-free" is a sentence that can mean several very different things, and only one of them is fraud.

**He might have claimed the exclusion and not been audited.** This is the big one. The IRS doesn't review every return. Someone can take an aggressive position, exclude the whole settlement, file, and never hear a word about it. That's not fraud — it's an unreviewed position. It's also not evidence the position is correct. Plenty of people drive 85 in a 65 and never get pulled over; that doesn't make it legal.

**His claim might genuinely have been different from yours.** Same dollar amount, same "settled the same way," but if his lawsuit was actually about a physical injury — a real one, pleaded and documented — then his exclusion could be perfectly proper while yours isn't. The origin of the claim is what matters, and you may not know what his pleadings said.

**He might have gotten a different allocation.** Maybe his agreement broke out a specific physical injury component with contemporaneous medical support. Maybe his attorney structured it differently. "Same way" from the outside can look very different on paper.

**Or he might have done something improper.** That's possible. But you'd need to know what he actually filed and what he actually claimed, and you don't.

The part I'd push back on: "either he committed fraud or you're wrong" assumes the tax system works by everyone getting audited and everything being adjudicated. It doesn't. It works on self-reporting plus spot checks. So "he got away with it" and "it's allowed" are two completely different statements, and you can't tell which one you're looking at from the outside.

What I'd actually do with this: ask him, specifically, what his claim was about and whether his agreement recited a physical injury. If he's vague or it turns out his case was a business dispute too, that tells you something. If it turns out he had a real injury claim, that tells you your situations aren't comparable.

But don't let his outcome drive your decision. His return isn't precedent, and if he took a position that doesn't hold up, the fact that he hasn't been caught yet doesn't protect you.
So what if I re-label the covenant consideration as "damages for physical suffering" in the contract — my lawyer friend says that's how it's done

That's the move that gets people in trouble, and your lawyer friend is describing something real but describing it wrong.

Yes, settlement agreements do allocate amounts to categories — that's normal and legitimate. Attorneys write recitals explaining what each payment is for, and those recitals matter. But there's a difference between *documenting* an allocation that reflects the actual claims and *inventing* one to change the tax result. The first is drafting. The second is what the case law calls a sham, and it's the single most common way these cases go bad.

Here's why relabeling the $140k non-compete as "damages for physical suffering" is especially weak:

**The origin of the claim controls, not the label.** Courts look at what the lawsuit was actually about — the pleadings, the discovery, the theory of liability, what the defendant was actually buying. If the $140k was consideration for you not competing, then it's payment for giving up future earnings, full stop. Calling it physical suffering damages in the contract doesn't change what the defendant got for the money. And the defendant's own conduct — did they get a non-compete? Did they enforce it? — will show what it was.

**A non-compete payment has an obvious non-tax reason to exist.** That's what makes relabeling so hard to defend. If the money was really for your insomnia, why is there a covenant not to compete attached to it? The structure itself contradicts the label.

**The IRS has seen this exact play.** Allocation language that appears only after tax planning, that doesn't match the pleadings, and that assigns a suspiciously round number to "physical suffering" is a known pattern. It invites scrutiny rather than avoiding it.

**And the downside is worse than just paying tax.** If the IRS decides the allocation was fabricated, you're looking at accuracy-related penalties, possibly civil fraud, and your lawyer friend's advice becomes evidence. The tax you'd owe on $240k is bad. The penalty stack on top of it is worse.

What legitimate allocation actually looks like: the agreement reflects claims that were genuinely made, supported by contemporaneous medical records and pleadings, with amounts that bear some relationship to the actual harm and the actual bargaining. If your case genuinely included a physical injury claim, then yes — allocate to it, and document why. If it didn't, no amount of drafting creates one.

The thing I'd say plainly: you're now three messages into looking for a way to make this non-taxable, and the answers keep coming back the same. That's usually a signal that the money is taxable and the real question is how to handle it. An hour with a tax attorney who sees the actual pleadings will settle this faster than any of this theorizing — and if there *is* a defensible physical injury component, they'll find it. If there isn't, you'll want to know that before you file, not after.
I hear you but I need one yes or no — can I tell my CPA the full $240k is non-taxable due to physical injury from this dispute

No.

You can tell your CPA whatever you want, but the answer to whether the full $240k is non-taxable due to physical injury is no. Insomnia and panic attacks don't meet the observable bodily harm standard, the $140k non-compete is compensation for giving up future earnings, and relabeling it in the contract doesn't change the origin of the claim.

Tell your CPA the truth: $240k settlement, $140k non-compete, $100k general release, and here's what the dispute was about. Let them tell you what's taxable. That's the conversation that actually protects you.
